faqs.a: Galloway Township sits in southern New Jersey on the Atlantic coast, between the Pine Barrens and the Shore, and the habitat in between the houses — Wharton State Forest edge and the Pine Barrens — gives wildlife food and cover a short run from rooflines, decks and crawlspaces. Sealing every entry we find, not just the obvious one, is what ends the cycle here.

faqs.q: Do groundhogs do real damage in Galloway Township?
faqs.a: They do in Atlantic County: burrows under decks, sheds and foundation edges undermine slabs and channel water against the house, and garden feeding is heavy from spring through fall. Our crew traps groundhogs at active burrows and backfills and screens the site afterward.

faqs.q: Our Galloway home sits closed half the year. How do we stop finding animals in it?
faqs.a: Closure is the invitation — a quiet house in the Barrens is a den with a roof. The fix is a whole-structure seal done while you are here: chimney capped, soffit and eave gaps closed in chew-proof metal, crawlspace and deck voids screened, and anything already in residence excluded first, with the attic cleaned so old scent does not advertise the place. Houses sealed that way stay empty of everything but people; houses that get a trap visit each spring just re-let the den annually. We can also document the seal so you have a record between visits.

faqs.q: Is the company licensed for wildlife work in New Jersey?
faqs.a: There is no New Jersey wildlife-control-operator license to hold — the state does not issue one, and you should be wary of any operator who claims otherwise. The legal basis for the work is the New Jersey Fish & Wildlife Game Code: we act as your designated agent as the property owner, and we hold Division of Fish & Wildlife depredation permits for the species that require them. That framework sets how each animal is handled, and we are glad to walk you through what it means for the animal on your property before any work starts.

Galloway Township.wildlife_intro:
Galloway Township gives our crew a Atlantic mix shaped by Wharton State Forest edge and the Pine Barrens and the housing around it. Raccoons and bats turn up constantly in Shore homes that sit closed between rentals, skunks work the sandy back-bay neighborhoods, and Pine Barrens-edge properties in Galloway and Hammonton see snakes and groundhogs along the tree line — and Galloway Township is squarely part of that pattern, with raccoons and gray squirrels in attics, skunks and opossums under decks, and seasonal bat work in the older rooflines.

Atlantic City and Pleasantville hold older brick and wood-frame blocks, the Shore towns mix raised beach houses and rentals, and inland Egg Harbor, Galloway and Hammonton are postwar and newer single-family subdivisions near the pines. In fall and winter, squirrels and rodents push into warm attics and wall voids in Galloway Township; spring brings denning raccoons and groundhog and skunk activity in yards, and summer is bat and mole season. Most Galloway Township jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing of every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

Galloway is the biggest township in New Jersey by land area, and most of it is Pine Barrens. Between the subdivisions stand miles of pitch pine and oak forest, cedar swamp along the Mullica and Great Egg Harbor drainages, and the Forsythe Refuge marshes at the township's eastern edge — which means the housing here never really leaves the woods. Raccoons den in chimneys from Smithville to Pomona, bats take the attics of the older farmhouses along the White Horse Pike corridor, and skunks and opossums work the sandy yards where the lawns run down to the treeline. The animal pressure on a Galloway home is not a neighbourhood problem; it is a forest-edge problem, and it renews itself every season.

The township's other signature is the part-time house. Shore-overflow homes, rental properties, and places that sit closed between the summer season and the holidays give bats and raccoons the undisturbed months they need, especially in the older stock around Smithville and the rural lanes inland. Our Galloway inspections assume a quiet house has been found by something until we prove otherwise — attic, chimney chase, crawlspace, and the voids under the decks that Barrens builders loved to leave unskirted on sandy posts.
Galloway Township.extendedBody:
Living at the edge of the Barrens

Galloway's sandy soil writes half of our call log. Moles tunnel it effortlessly and are in every lawn not separated from the woods; skunks dig the same sand under porches and shed slabs; groundhogs hold the sunny edges where subdivision meets farm field. The pine canopy over the older subdivisions is a squirrel highway that ends at the soffit line, and the cedar swamps keep mosquito-season bats fed and close. On a Galloway property we read the treeline as part of the inspection — how close the woods stand, where the canopy touches the roof, which outbuildings bridge the gap — because the house is rarely the animal's first stop; it is the last one on a route that starts in the forest.

How this work is authorized in New Jersey

New Jersey does not issue a wildlife-control-operator license, so any company that calls itself state-licensed for this work is inventing a credential. What the law provides instead: our operators work as the property owner's designated agent under the New Jersey Fish & Wildlife Game Code, and hold Division depredation permits for the species that require one. That is the honest framing, and it comes with real obligations — including how each species may be handled and where it may be released. Raccoons and skunks, the state's rabies concerns, are dealt with by exclusion and sealing, and the sealing is what we are actually selling: the animal is today's problem, the open soffit is next year's.

Stockton, Smithville, and the rural lanes

Around Stockton University and the denser Pomona subdivisions, the calls run suburban — squirrels, raccoons, the occasional rat run along the commercial corridors. In Smithville and the farm lanes inland, they run rural: bats in tall farmhouse attics, raccoons in barn-adjacent chimneys, groundhogs under the outbuildings. Same township, two playbooks; the inspection tells us which one your property needs.

faqs.q: Can you get a raccoon family out of a Mays Landing chimney?
faqs.a: Yes, and spring families are handled as families. A mother raccoon picks an uncapped flue because it mimics a hollow tree, and pups too young to climb are never sealed in or left behind — we check the flue first, reunite or remove the litter with the mother, and fit a proper cap once the chimney is empty. The village chimneys are mostly older brick, and several have lost their caps to storms over the years. Raccoons are a New Jersey rabies-vector species, so the work is done with that caution built in.

faqs.q: Groundhogs keep raiding my Mays Landing garden — what actually works?
faqs.a: Fences alone rarely do; groundhogs climb and dig. What works is removing the animals that have claimed the yard and closing the den they commute from, which is usually under a deck, shed, or brush line rather than in the open. River-bottom gardens here sit on soft, diggable soil, and a resident groundhog usually dens under the nearest shed or porch rather than out in the open. Trapping is set at the burrow mouth, and once the site is clear we backfill and screen it. A garden next to an occupied burrow is a salad bar with a commute of about ten feet.

Mays Landing.wildlife_intro:
Mays Landing still reads as a river village: the Great Egg Harbor River curls past the old courthouse blocks, Lake Lenape sits at the west end, and streets of 1800s and early-1900s houses give way to postwar subdivisions along Routes 40 and 50. That older housing is where the work concentrates. Raccoons den in uncapped chimneys on the village streets, big brown bats summer in the tall attics of the riverfront-era homes, and groundhogs work the garden lots that back onto open ground toward Weymouth and the river bottom.

Masonry chimneys deserve a slow look. Mortar joints crumble at the crown, flashing lifts where the stack meets the roof, and an uncapped flue reads to a raccoon like a hollow tree. Sealing here is masonry work as much as animal work: a correctly sized cap, repointed joints where they have failed, and flashing reset so water stays out along with the wildlife. Brick and stone stacks on older houses often hide a second, unused flue that nobody remembers — exactly the sort of quiet, warm shaft a denning animal chooses in March. In Mays Landing the inspection always includes the flue and the river-side foundation wall, because those are the two routes village animals have used for a century.

faqs.q: What should I do about a skunk under my Pleasantville porch?
faqs.a: Keep dogs inside at dusk and do not try to block the opening while the skunk is home — that traps it and guarantees a spray. Our crew removes skunks from under porches and decks in Pleasantville with covered, low-stress handling, then screens the opening so the next skunk cannot move in.

faqs.q: Are bats a problem in Pleasantville homes?
faqs.a: Yes — older rooflines and quiet attics in Pleasantville host summer colonies, and in Atlantic County the work is exclusion only, timed around the maternity season. Our crew maps every entry, fits one-way exits in the right window, and seals the building behind the bats.

faqs.q: Rats keep coming back to our Pleasantville block. What actually ends it?
faqs.a: Sealing your building — that is the only part fully in your control, and it is the part that works. Rats here travel the laterals and foundation lines of the whole block, so a trapped-out house with an open sill or a broken cleanout is re-let within the season. We trap the active animals, then find and close your entries and identify the defects (like a cracked lateral) that need a plumber, with photos and a written account you can also use with your neighbours — block-wide, the houses that seal are the houses that stop calling.

faqs.q: A raccoon had kits in our Pleasantville chimney. Can the family just be moved?
faqs.a: The family comes out — that part we handle, mother and kits together, timed so the young are not separated. What the law does not allow is carrying them off to release somewhere else; New Jersey's Game Code does not work that way, and raccoons are a rabies-concern species besides. The durable answer is what happens after: a proper chimney cap and the roofline gaps closed, because a sow raccoon returns to a proven den every spring and teaches the address to her daughters. Seal it once and the tradition ends.

Pleasantville is Atlantic City's old neighbour, not its suburb — a dense little city of pre-war and postwar housing standing on the mainland side of the bay, and its wildlife work is city work. Norway rats run the older blocks, the alley lines, and the commercial corridors; raccoons den in the chimneys and attics of the tight-packed housing; skunks live under porches on nearly every street; and the back-bay marshes at the city's edge keep the whole population fed and moving. Where Galloway's problem is the forest, Pleasantville's is the block: shared walls, shared fences, and animals that treat five backyards as one territory.

The bay side tells the second half of the story. Lakes Bay and the marsh creeks border the city, and the neighbourhoods toward the water get the marsh animals with the tide — raccoons working the bulkhead lines, opossums under the low decks, rats along the drainage. Inland, the older housing stock itself is the habitat: a century of porches, additions, and patch repairs on tight lots means every elevation of a Pleasantville home has a junction, and every junction is a candidate entry.
Pleasantville.extendedBody:
Block-by-block work: rats, raccoons, and the porches of Pleasantville

Rat work here is building work. The older commercial corridors and the dense residential blocks share sewer laterals, hollow foundations, and fence-line runs, and a rat population belongs to the block, not to one address — which is why we inspect and report the whole picture: the lateral defects, the open foundation gaps, the food sources in the alley. Trapping drops the numbers; sealing the entries at your address is what keeps your house out of the next cycle. Raccoons take the roofs above the same streets, denning in chimneys each spring, and skunks take the porches below them. A Pleasantville job typically touches all three levels of the house in one visit, because the animals certainly do.

The legal basis for the work in New Jersey

New Jersey has no wildlife-control-operator license — the state does not issue one for this work. Our operators act as your designated agent under the New Jersey Fish & Wildlife Game Code, holding Division depredation permits where a species requires one. For rabies-concern species like raccoons and skunks, the method is exclusion and sealing: the animal out, the entry closed in metal, and the den made useless. Any company promising to simply carry a raccoon across town and let it go is promising something the Game Code does not allow them to sell you.

The bay edge

Toward Lakes Bay, the inspections add the marsh: bulkhead burrows, drainage outfalls, and the low deck voids the opossums and skunks prefer. Homes on the marsh blocks get a foundation pass the inland streets do not need, because high water pushes marsh animals up against the houses several times a year, and the ones that find an open crawlspace tend to stay.

faqs.q: What snakes turn up around Hammonton, and which are dangerous?
faqs.a: This is Pine Barrens snake country. The northern pine snake — state-Threatened, a burrower in sandy soil — is the species people meet most dramatically, and it is protected: identification and referral, never handling. A separate southern population of timber rattlesnakes also persists in the Barrens. Sandy Hammonton soil is exactly what a pine snake wants for burrowing, so a big pale snake near a woodpile here deserves a photograph and a wide berth, not a shovel. Common harmless residents include black racers, garter snakes, and eastern hognose, which plays dead theatrically. Non-listed snakes found inside a home can be caught and released outdoors within 200 meters.

faqs.q: A groundhog is burrowing under my Hammonton foundation — how bad is that?
faqs.a: Worse than it looks. A groundhog burrow system runs many feet with several chambers, and soil removed from under a slab or footing leaves voids that crack concrete and channel water against the foundation. In Hammonton the burrow undermining a barn slab or a farmhouse addition is the common version of this call, and the field edge behind the building is usually where the second entrance sits. We trap at the active entrances, then backfill and screen the site so the next groundhog inherits a closed burrow. Groundhogs are on New Jersey's rabies-vector list — one more reason not to corner one yourself.

Hammonton.wildlife_intro:
Hammonton calls itself the Blueberry Capital of the World, and the working farms that ring the town shape its wildlife calls as much as the houses do. Along the White Horse Pike and the downtown blocks the housing is older frame and brick; out past the town line, farmhouses and ranch homes sit between blueberry fields and the pitch-pine edge of the Barrens. Groundhogs commute between field edges and foundation burrows, raccoons work barn lofts and chimneys, and at the sandy Barrens fringe the occasional pine snake sighting sends a homeowner indoors to make a phone call.

On farm and acreage properties the house is only part of the job. Barns shelter raccoon families in haylofts, groundhogs undermine run-in sheds and fence lines, and skunks take up residence under equipment sheds where they are discovered by smell. We plan the property as a whole — which structures to proof, which burrows to treat, where trapping effort actually pays — instead of chasing one animal at a time. Grain and feed storage gets the same attention as the house foundation, because spilled feed is usually what drew the animals to the buildings in the first place. Hammonton jobs are quoted as a property, not a single structure, because the barn, the shed, and the house usually share the same animals.
